title: Opportunity Evaluation under Risky Conditions: The Cognitive Processes of Entrepreneurs

source.title: Opportunity Evaluation under Risky Conditions: The Cognitive Processes of Entrepreneurs
source.authors: Hean Tat Keh, Maw Der Foo, Boon Chong Lim

studies.title: Survey · Evaluating a new venture opportunity

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Why do entrepreneurs evaluate the same risky opportunity differently, and does perceived risk help explain those differences?

fields.label: What the paper covers
fields.value: A questionnaire survey of Singapore entrepreneurs and a common business vignette, with regression-based hypothesis tests.

fields.label: Across the paper
fields.value: Entrepreneurs who perceived less risk evaluated the opportunity more positively. Perceived risk statistically accounted for part of the association with illusion of control.

fields.label: Expectation or comparison
fields.value: The authors predicted that perceived risk would relate negatively to evaluation and examined whether it linked cognitive biases to opportunity evaluation.

fields.label: Interpretation and limits
fields.value: The survey measures individual differences rather than randomly assigning them. The paper’s regression mediation result does not establish causal mediation.
fields.derivation: Scope of the published evidence and, where linked, differences from the Bench adaptation.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: 77 completed surveys from entrepreneurs were available. Respondents evaluated a hypothetical opportunity. Measures cover risk perception, opportunity evaluation, overconfidence, belief in small samples, planning fallacy and illusion of control.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: The paper defines opportunity evaluation and perceived risk as distinct outcomes. It checks relationships with the four cognitive factors while including age and risk propensity as controls.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Three regression models test which factors relate to risk perception and opportunity evaluation, then add perceived risk to the evaluation model.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: Perceived risk was negatively associated with evaluation (b=−0.50, p<.001 in Model 3). Illusion of control predicted lower perceived risk (b=−0.76, p<.01); its evaluation coefficient fell when perceived risk was added. The authors report weaker evidence for a direct small-samples association (b=1.17, p<.06 in Model 2).
